analysis.one_liner: Requires insurers to base drug coinsurance on the net price after rebates, not the inflated list price.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor vote and died at the end of the 116th Congress with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Many insured people with high deductibles pay a percentage of a drug's list price — the inflated sticker price before rebates — while their insurer actually pays a much lower net price after manufacturer rebates and discounts. This bill would require private insurance plans to calculate a patient's coinsurance based on that lower net price, so patients share in the savings from negotiated rebates instead of paying a share of a price nobody really pays.
analysis.who_benefits: Insured people with deductibles or coinsurance obligations for prescription drugs, especially those on expensive brand-name drugs where the gap between list price and net price after rebates is largest. Their out-of-pocket payments would be calculated on the price their plan actually pays, lowering their cost-sharing [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires group health plans and insurers to set any coinsurance obligation for a prescription drug based on the drug's net price — the list price minus all rebates, discounts, and concessions — so no patient payment is a percentage of the list price [S3].
It applies when an enrollee has an unmet deductible or another coinsurance obligation for drug benefits, the situations where list-price-based cost-sharing hits patients hardest [S2].
Plans could still charge flat copayments, as long as the copayment is not tied to a percentage of the drug's cost [S2] [S3].
It would take effect for plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2021 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and pharmacy benefit managers would bear the adjustment: rebates they negotiate would have to flow into lower patient cost-sharing rather than staying with the plan. Insurers might respond with higher premiums or higher flat copays to make up the difference, and the bill does not directly lower drug list prices themselves.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and pharmacy benefit managers

drawbacks.text: The bill addresses only how coinsurance is calculated; it does not lower drug prices themselves, so plans could offset the mandate through higher premiums or larger flat copays (which the bill still permits) [S2] [S3].

Because net prices after rebates are often confidential and settled retrospectively, plans and pharmacy benefit managers would need new accounting to compute a patient's share at the pharmacy counter, and disputes over rebate pass-through could create administrative cost [S3].
The requirement applies only to private group and individual coverage; it does not reach uninsured people or change Medicare or Medicaid cost-sharing [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients on expensive drugs with percentage-based coinsurance, the benefit could be substantial, since rebates on brand-name drugs are often large and today's cost-sharing is computed on the inflated list price. The main cost is administrative complexity for insurers and the risk that plans recapture some of the savings through premiums or copays. On balance a genuine consumer protection, though narrower than full drug-pricing reform.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee, where it sat with no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote, and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Gallagher introduced the bill on July 17, 2019, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S5].
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, where no further action was recorded [S5].
The bill drew no cosponsors [S4], and the committee never held a markup or sent it to the floor before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and pharmacy benefit managers are better off: rebates they negotiate continue to be calculated against patient cost-sharing based on list prices, and no rule requires them to pass those rebates through to patients. Patients on high-cost drugs keep paying coinsurance on inflated list prices.

for.name: Rep. Mike Gallagher
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require drug coinsurance to be based on net price after rebates.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair Rep. Frank Pallone, D-NJ)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral: no hearing, no markup, and no vote, leaving the bill to die in committee.

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican sponsor introduced the bill with no cosponsors from either party, and no votes were ever recorded, so the partisan shape of potential support or opposition cannot be determined from the record.

industries.note: PBMs negotiate the rebates and discounts that this bill would define as the net price for patient cost-sharing. Requiring coinsurance to be computed on the net price would push part of those rebated savings to patients instead of leaving them in the PBM-and-plan chain [S3].

Insurers would have to base patient coinsurance on the net price they actually pay, reducing what they collect from enrollees at the point of sale; they could partially recoup through premiums or flat copays, which the bill still allows [S2] [S3].

Manufacturers set high list prices while offering large hidden rebates. If patient cost-sharing were based on the lower net price, the consumer-facing penalty of high list prices would shrink, pressuring the high-list, high-rebate pricing structure [S2] [S3].
